title: Sex life: Retirement planning for sex workers
gist: Sydney-based sex worker Tilly Lawless reflects on retirement planning in her industry: career sex workers mostly exit via marriage or into managing brothels because discrimination limits other jobs, and she argues rights groups that bar former managers are wrong while career options after sex work remain narrow.

insights.claim: According to Lawless, most career sex workers she has worked with either became 'trophy wives' or eventually moved into running a brothel or parlour, as opposed to those dabbling while studying.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Illustrates how labour-market discrimination channels workers into narrow post-career paths within the same sector.
insights.quote: have either become trophy wives or transitioned eventually to running a place

insights.claim: There is a clear pipeline from sex worker to manager of sex workers, driven both by industry experience and by discrimination that makes other employment hard to obtain.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Stigma limits labour mobility, concentrating management roles among former workers.
insights.quote: There is a clear pipeline from working girl to manager of working girls

insights.claim: Ageing sex workers adapt rather than quit, for example shifting to dominatrix-only work and dropping full service, or stopping night shifts.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.quote: shifting to only dominatrix work and eliminating full service

insights.claim: Some sex worker rights organisations bar current or former brothel managers from membership; Lawless argues this is untenable because many owners still see clients and face the same treatment from clients and the state.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Signals internal fault lines in sex-work advocacy that shape lobbying on decriminalisation and licensing.
insights.quote: which is why some bar sex workers who are or have been brothel managers from becoming members
insights.locator: I am asked often if this

insights.claim: Lawless argues the industry needs more ethical people in owner, manager and receptionist roles rather than demonising them, and that until post-sex-work career options broaden it is unfair to criticise ageing workers for taking those jobs.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.quote: Until we broaden the career opportunities for women after sex work
insights.locator: I am asked often if this

themes.theme: Cultural depiction of ageing sex workers

insights.claim: On-screen sex workers are usually shown young and dying of disease, addiction or violence; Ken Loach's 1966 film Cathy Come Home is a rare depiction of a former sex worker with a life after work.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.quote: we so rarely see an aged or former sex worker on screen
